explanation: Fires on mid-word subword pieces inside rare or foreign proper names, odd technical names and multi-byte character fragments (e.g. 'G[iar]utana', 'But[t]igieg', 'Z[ope]Data', CJK byte pieces), plus a few specific syntactic spots such as '{' after 'const' in JS destructuring and ' v' in legal case captions ('X v. Y'). Ordinary common words barely activate it. There is no single shared semantic theme.

Fires on the second or later item of a list or coordination, especially the token ' and' joining two or more named things ('students and subjects', 'radiotherapy and chemotherapy', 'X, Y, and Z'). It also fires on mid-word pieces of rare proper or taxonomic names (Kot[aku], Radv[ili]škis, formos[anus]). Generic text outside lists is weak.

Fires on the comma right after the first item of an enumerated list of nouns (places, brands, materials, symptoms: 'Golden Gate Bridge, Alcatraz', 'Whirlpool, Kenmore'), anticipating more items to come. Commas later in a list or before 'and' are weaker, and non-list commas are weak or zero.

Fires on tokens inside whitespace-aligned, column-style tabular text in code or plain-text tables (the column header 'Sth[Am]' is far above everything else), and moderately on tokens in code formatting such as docblock tags, class braces, timestamps in tables and license-header comment closers. Prose is near zero.

Fires on the first item of an enumeration right where a list starts, typically after 'for', '(', 'such as', 'of' or a dash: 'has [0] or more', 'flood[s], hurricanes', 'MMP-[1], -2', '([food], water', 'with [copy], paste'. The item token is what fires, and it needs the context to signal that more coordinated items follow.

Fires on structural or boilerplate positions in documents: the '======' separator lines in Hacker News-style comment dumps, the ' *' continuation lines and indentation in code license and docblock comments, and formulaic tokens in boilerplate prose ('hereby granted', 'by way of example', 'The record'). It also fires on assorted mid-sentence tokens with no clear common thread, so the picture is mixed.

Fires on tokens inside runs of uninformative or hard-to-segment text: long digit strings of zeros, multi-byte CJK, Devanagari or mojibake fragments, and subword pieces of foreign or rare names and Latin words (Sol[an]um, Sh[al]). Weaker on paragraph-ending '.\n\n'. The common factor seems to be byte-level or subword fragments, not meaning.

Fires on the token just before a ' :' separator in ternary expressions, object-literal key/value pairs, C++ initializer or inheritance lists and legal-caption colon columns ('? [a] : b', '"idiom["] :', 'Cow(int age[)] : Animal'). In other words it predicts that a spaced colon comes next. It also fires weakly on French articles ('un', 'dé'). JSON keys with no space before the colon are weak.

Fires in code on identifiers tied to results, status, errors and messages from a request or operation: lbl[Message], response.getStatus, hResult, 'message': str(ex), response.status, err, form_errors, success callbacks. Also moderate on related prose such as 'request success'. Code identifiers unrelated to result or error handling are weak.

Fires on a token inside a fixed multi-word expression or collocation where the following word is highly predictable: 'in one [way] or another', 'at least [one] direction', 'In [order] to', 'In [light] of', 'people [with] the surname', 'just a [few]', 'found [the] right place'. It is strongest at the pivot word of the idiom. Free, unpredictable continuations are weak.

Fires on a mix: CJK (Chinese/Japanese) word tokens, boilerplate phrases such as 'agreed [to] in writing' in Apache license headers and 'Copy [may] not be', and ' but' after 'looking for a solution'. Other common function words in various contexts also fire. No single shared concept is visible.

Fires on tokens expressing alternatives, fallbacks or conditionals: the ternary operator (the word 'Operator', '?' and ':'), ISNULL, failover, backup/back-up, default values, 'either', 'else', 'try', a diesel generator as backup power. Unrelated tokens are weak.

Fires on subword pieces inside Devanagari (Hindi) words, and more weakly on subword or name tokens in Italian text and in Italian or South-Asian personal names (Gi[ud]ice, Gi[ac]omo, Paolo, Rath[ore], An[sh]ul). Common English words do not fire.

Fires on internal subword pieces of biochemical and chemical compound names, such as 'phosph', 'osph', 'at', 'eth', 'uran' or 'clid' inside farnesyl, phosphatase, guanine, cyclophosphamide and neuraminidase. It is strongest in the middle of long IUPAC-like drug, enzyme or metabolite names. Stray offshoots include 'contributor [license]' in Apache headers.
